questions.stem: On a very hot day, a person begins sweating heavily and their skin appears flushed (red). Which physiological mechanisms are at work to cool the body?

options.text: Vasoconstriction and shivering to generate heat
Vasodilation (blood vessels near the skin surface widen) to radiate heat, and sweating to cool the skin by evaporation
Erector muscles contract, raising body hair to trap warm air
The hypothalamus shuts down to prevent overheating

questions.explanation: When the body is too hot, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate (vasodilation), bringing more blood closer to the surface where heat can radiate away. This causes the flushed appearance. Sweat glands produce sweat, which evaporates from the skin surface, removing heat energy.

questions.stem: A hiker gets caught in freezing rain and begins shivering uncontrollably. What is the purpose of shivering in thermoregulation?

options.text: Shivering squeezes blood towards the skin surface to warm it
Rapid involuntary muscle contractions generate heat from increased respiration in the muscle cells
Shivering opens the sweat glands to release warm fluid
Shivering signals to the brain that the person needs to find shelter

questions.explanation: Shivering is the rapid, involuntary contraction and relaxation of skeletal muscles. This muscle activity requires increased respiration, which releases energy as heat, helping to raise the body's core temperature when it drops below the normal 37°C set point.

questions.stem: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat. A patient has damage to their hypothalamus. What effect would this have on their temperature regulation?

options.text: They would maintain a perfectly constant body temperature
They would struggle to detect temperature changes and coordinate appropriate responses, leading to dangerous temperature fluctuations
Their body temperature would permanently increase to 40°C
They would only be able to regulate temperature using behavioural methods

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus monitors blood temperature and coordinates the body's thermoregulatory responses (vasodilation/vasoconstriction, sweating, shivering). If damaged, it cannot detect temperature deviations or send appropriate signals to effectors, leading to potentially dangerous fluctuations in core body temperature.

questions.stem: During vasoconstriction in cold conditions, blood is diverted away from the skin surface. Why does this help conserve heat?

options.text: Less blood at the skin surface means less heat is lost by radiation to the environment
Vasoconstriction generates heat through friction in the blood vessels
Vasoconstriction increases sweating to warm the skin
Blood is diverted to the lungs to be warmed by breathing

questions.explanation: In cold conditions, arterioles supplying skin capillaries constrict (narrow), diverting blood deeper into the body. With less warm blood flowing near the skin surface, less heat is lost by radiation to the cooler environment, helping to maintain core body temperature.

questions.stem: A patient has a fever of 39°C due to infection. Their body is shivering even though their temperature is above normal. Why does this happen?

options.text: The infection has destroyed the body's ability to sense temperature
During fever, the hypothalamus raises the set point; the body shivers because its current temperature is below this new, higher set point
Shivering is caused directly by the bacteria, not by the nervous system
The patient is actually cold because the infection lowers body temperature

questions.explanation: During a fever, chemicals released by the immune system cause the hypothalamus to temporarily raise its temperature set point (e.g., to 39°C). The body then behaves as if it is 'too cold' compared to this new set point, triggering shivering and vasoconstriction to raise the temperature further.
